stem:
A 15-year-old reports eight-day periods with flooding since menarche. She has also had recurrent prolonged nosebleeds since childhood and bled for hours after a dental extraction. Her mother describes similar symptoms. She has no joint bleeds and takes no medicines. The GP obtains the following results.

| Test | Result | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | 103 g/L | 120–155 |
| Ferritin | 8 micrograms/L | 15–150 |
| Platelets | 276 × 10⁹/L | 150–450 |
| INR | 1.0 | 0.9–1.2 |
| APTT | 31 seconds | 25–35 |

Which underlying diagnosis best explains the bleeding history?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Anovulation is common after menarche but cannot account for childhood epistaxis, dental bleeding and a similarly affected parent.

options.label: B
options.explanation: von Willebrand disease can cause mucocutaneous and menstrual bleeding with normal platelet count, INR and APTT. The iron deficiency is a consequence, not a full explanation.

options.label: C
options.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency usually affects coagulation tests, particularly PT/INR, and does not fit the stable familial mucosal-bleeding pattern.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia requires a reduced platelet count and does not explain this lifelong familial pattern with normal platelets.

options.label: E
options.explanation: Haemophilia typically causes deep muscle or joint bleeding. This mucosal pattern in successive generations, including females, is more consistent with von Willebrand disease.

context: A normal platelet count and routine coagulation screen do not exclude von Willebrand disease. Lifelong mucosal bleeding and family history matter when assessing heavy periods.
